directions: The observations and findings in this Judgment are only for the purpose of reaching the conclusion as to whether charge under Section 326A of IPC has been correctly framed and whether the trial court committed an error in rejecting the application for discharge under Section 326A of IPC.
The trial shall be conducted uninfluenced by any of the observations on the merits of the matter.

issue.issue_text: Whether the title of a statutory provision can control its contents in the event of a conflict between the plain expressions in the provision and the indicated title.

law.law_text: The primary rule of statutory interpretation is the 'plain meaning rule,' which dictates that the legislative intent must be found in the plain and unambiguous words used in the statute itself.
The title or heading of a statutory provision is considered only a broad and general indicator of the subject matter it deals with.

A title's relevance depends on the clarity of the provision's text. If the text is clear and unambiguous, the title is irrelevant. If the text is ambiguous, the title can be used as an aid to interpretation.

application.application_text: The Court established a clear hierarchy between a provision's text and its title. The plain language of the provision is superior.

Applying this hierarchy, the Court determined that in the event of a direct conflict between the plain expressions in a provision and its title, the title cannot control or override the meaning of the text.

The Court reasoned that because the language employed in a statute is the determinative factor of legislative intent, the clear text must be given effect over its more general and potentially misleading title.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the title of a statutory provision cannot control its contents. In a conflict between the plain, unambiguous language of a provision and its title, the language of the provision must prevail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the title of a statutory provision can control its contents in the event of a conflict between the plain expressions in the provision and the indicated title.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that they could not be charged under Section 326A of the IPC because the injury caused was simple, not grievous hurt, as per the medical report.

This argument implies that the nature of the resulting injury (grievous hurt, as suggested by the section's context or title) is a necessary element for the charge, and the plain text of the provision should be controlled by this requirement.

The appellant relied on two High Court decisions (Laddu Ram v. State of Rajasthan and M. Siluvai Murugan @ Murugan v. State) to support the view that the absence of grievous hurt precludes a charge under Section 326A.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's arguments. However, the court's reasoning, which supports the respondent's position, is that the plain meaning of a statute must be given effect.
It was argued implicitly that if the language of the provision is simple and unambiguous, it should be interpreted as such, without giving any weightage to the headings or titles of the paragraphs.

cases.case_name: Prakash Nath Khanna and Anr. v. Commissioner of Income Tax and Anr.
cases.principle: Headings or titles of sections have a limited role in statutory construction; they are broad indicators of the subject matter but cannot control the meaning of plain and clear language in the provision itself.

cases.case_name: Raichurmatham Prabhakar and Another v. Rawatmal Dugar
cases.principle: The title of a provision does not control its contents, especially when the provision's language is plain and unambiguous. In case of a conflict, the plain language of the provision prevails over the title.

cases.case_name: Union of India (UOI) and Another v. National Federation of the Blind and Others
cases.principle: The title of a provision does not control its contents, especially when the provision's language is plain and unambiguous. In case of a conflict, the plain language of the provision prevails over the title.

cases.case_name: Lenigh Valley Coal Co. v. Yensavage
cases.principle: Statutes should not be construed like mathematical theorems; their words must be interpreted with an understanding of the purposes behind them.

cases.case_name: Union of India v. Filip Tiago De Gama of Vedem Vasco De Gama
cases.principle: The primary rule of construction is that legislative intent must be found in the words used by the legislature itself, focusing on what has been said, not what might have been intended.

cases.case_name: Padma Sundara Rao v. State of T.N.
cases.principle: The primary rule of construction is that legislative intent must be found in the words used by the legislature itself, focusing on what has been said, not what might have been intended.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When interpreting a statute, the plain and unambiguous language of a provision is the determinative factor of legislative intent and must be given effect. In the event of a conflict between the plain language of the provision and its heading or title, the heading or title cannot control the meaning that is clearly discernible from the language of the provision itself.
obiter: Headings or titles prefixed to sections may be referred to as broad and general indicators of the subject matter, or to explain ambiguities, but they play a limited role in statutory construction.
Statutes should be construed not as theorems of Euclid, but words must be construed with some imagination of the purposes which lie behind them.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The plain and unambiguous language of a statutory provision must be given effect, and the court cannot read anything into it that is not present. The title or heading of a section cannot control the meaning of the provision itself if the text is clear; it serves as an aid to understanding but does not override the explicit language.
legal_tests_applied: The Plain Meaning Rule: It is a settled law that while interpreting any provision of a statute the plain meaning has to be given effect and if language therein is simple and unambiguous, there is no need to traverse beyond the same.

Rule on Statutory Headings: If the language of the relevant section gives a simple meaning and message, it should be interpreted in such a way and there is no need to give any weightage to headings of those paragraphs.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument, which sought to use the title of Section 326A IPC to import a requirement that the resulting injury must be 'grievous hurt', failed because it contradicts the principle that the plain text of a statute is paramount.
The court cannot read words into a statutory provision that are not there, and the appellant's interpretation would require doing so based solely on the section's title.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position prevailed because it aligned with the well-settled legal principle that a court must give effect to the plain meaning of a statute when its language is simple and unambiguous.
The court affirmed that the title of a statutory provision is not a controlling factor and should not be given weightage over the clear language of the section itself.
